timed_cues.label: After a meal
timed_cues.script: Start just after a meal. Carbohydrate is digested into glucose, which is absorbed through the gut and enters the circulation. Blood glucose rises. That rise is not a problem. It is the signal that tells the body that fuel has arrived and is ready to be used.

timed_cues.label: Pancreatic sensing
timed_cues.script: Beta cells in the pancreatic islets detect the rising glucose and release insulin into the bloodstream. Insulin travels to tissues, particularly muscle and fat, and binds to insulin receptors on the cell surface. Think of insulin as the message: fuel has arrived, so use it now and store what is left.

timed_cues.label: Receptor signalling
timed_cues.script: Binding activates the insulin receptor and starts a signalling chain inside the cell: IRS one, PI3 kinase, then Akt. The key endpoint here is GLUT4. Vesicles carrying GLUT4 move to and fuse with the cell membrane. Glucose can then enter the cell, where it is used to make ATP or stored as glycogen.

timed_cues.label: Negative feedback
timed_cues.script: As glucose enters cells, the blood level falls. Beta cells respond by reducing insulin release. Glucose rises, insulin rises, glucose is handled, then both settle again.

stages.script: Normal insulin physiology after a meal.

Before going any further, separate type one from type two diabetes. They are not the same disease. In type one diabetes, the primary problem is loss of pancreatic beta cells, so insulin becomes severely deficient. In type two diabetes, insulin is still being produced, often in large amounts initially, but the tissues respond poorly to it. That is insulin resistance. Only later does beta-cell function usually become insufficient for the amount of insulin resistance. Both can cause hyperglycaemia, but the route to hyperglycaemia is different. Keep those two pathways separate as we go through the rest of the lesson.

Start with type one diabetes. The initiating problem is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells. As beta-cell mass falls, insulin production falls. Eventually there is not enough insulin to signal the fed state properly. Now remember what insulin normally says to the body: glucose is available, use it, store it, and stop producing more fuel. In type one diabetes that message disappears. So the problem is much bigger than simply having a high glucose concentration.

stages.chapter: Type 1 — the body enters a fasting state
stages.script: Now follow the consequences of severe insulin deficiency. In muscle and adipose tissue, insulin-dependent glucose uptake falls. In the liver, insulin is no longer suppressing glucose production, while glucagon is relatively unopposed, so glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis continue. Blood glucose therefore rises from both sides: less glucose is being cleared and more glucose is being produced. At the same time, insulin is no longer restraining lipolysis. Fatty acids are released from adipose tissue and delivered to the liver, where they are converted into ketone bodies. So the key paradox is this: there is plenty of glucose in the blood, but the body behaves metabolically as though it is starving. That is why type one diabetes can cause rapid weight loss and, when insulin deficiency is severe, diabetic ketoacidosis.

Now reset and look at type two diabetes separately. Here the early problem is not absent insulin. Insulin is present, and often raised, but muscle, liver and adipose tissue respond less effectively to it. In muscle and fat, insulin signalling produces less effective glucose uptake. In the liver, insulin is less able to suppress glucose production. The pancreas senses that glucose is harder to control and compensates by releasing more insulin. So early type two diabetes is often a state of insulin resistance plus compensatory hyperinsulinaemia.

For a while, extra insulin can compensate for insulin resistance and keep glucose near normal. That is why insulin resistance can exist for years before overt diabetes appears. But the beta cells are being asked to produce more insulin continuously. Over time, in susceptible people, beta-cell function declines and insulin secretion becomes inadequate for the degree of resistance. At that point blood glucose rises persistently. So type two diabetes is best thought of as two processes together: insulin resistance first, followed by insufficient beta-cell compensation.

Now derive the symptoms properly. Start with the effects of hyperglycaemia, which can happen in both type one and type two diabetes. As plasma glucose rises, more glucose is filtered through the glomerulus into the renal tubule. The proximal tubule normally reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose, but its transport capacity is finite. Once the filtered glucose load exceeds that capacity, glucose remains in the tubular fluid and appears in the urine. That is glycosuria. Now ask why glycosuria causes polyuria. Glucose is osmotically active, so glucose left inside the renal tubule keeps water in the tubular fluid. Less water is reabsorbed and urine volume increases. That is an osmotic diuresis, and clinically that gives you polyuria. Continued urinary water loss reduces circulating volume and raises effective osmolality. The hypothalamus detects this, thirst increases, and the patient drinks more. That is polydipsia. So the chain is not something to memorise: hyperglycaemia, increased filtered glucose load, saturation of tubular glucose reabsorption, glycosuria, osmotic diuresis, polyuria, dehydration, then polydipsia. Now separate out what happens in severe type one diabetes. When insulin is profoundly deficient, lipolysis accelerates. Free fatty acids reach the liver and are converted into ketone bodies, particularly beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. These acids release hydrogen ions, bicarbonate is consumed buffering them, and a metabolic acidosis develops. The respiratory centre responds to the acidaemia by increasing ventilation. The breaths become deep and often rapid so that more carbon dioxide is exhaled. Lowering carbon dioxide lowers carbonic acid and partially compensates for the metabolic acidosis. That deep laboured breathing is Kussmaul respiration. It is not simply breathlessness from diabetes; it is respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. The same severe insulin deficiency also explains rapid weight loss. Some of the weight loss is water, but the body is also breaking down fat and protein because the normal anabolic insulin signal is missing. Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain in DKA arise in the context of ketonaemia, acidosis and dehydration. Fruity or acetone breath occurs because acetoacetate can form volatile acetone, which is exhaled. So keep the mechanisms separate: polyuria and polydipsia come mainly from hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis, whereas Kussmaul breathing, marked ketosis and rapid catabolic weight loss point toward severe insulin deficiency and DKA, classically type one diabetes.

stages.chapter: Diagnosis — first prove diabetes, then classify it
stages.script: Diagnosis has two separate questions. First: is this diabetes? That is answered by demonstrating hyperglycaemia using appropriate plasma glucose or HbA1c criteria in the clinical context. Second: what type of diabetes is this? In a child, the history, tempo, body habitus, presence of ketosis, autoantibodies and sometimes C-peptide help distinguish type one from type two and from less common forms. And if the child is unwell, there is a third urgent question: is there DKA? That requires ketones and acid-base assessment, not simply a high glucose value.

Finally, treatment follows directly from the mechanism. In type one diabetes, the central defect is severe insulin deficiency, so insulin must be replaced. In type two diabetes, the central early problem is insulin resistance, so treatment aims to reduce glucose load, improve insulin sensitivity and reduce inappropriate hepatic glucose output; additional therapies or insulin may be needed as beta-cell function declines. So keep the distinction clear from beginning to end. Type one: insulin is missing. Type two: insulin is resisted, then beta-cell compensation becomes inadequate. Both raise glucose, but for different reasons.
